bigPicture: Two forces are pulling on the world's markets this morning. In the US, Federal Reserve officials opened the door to a half-point interest-rate rise in December after hotter-than-expected inflation, pushing the 10-year US government bond yield to about 5% and Wall Street lower, with Nvidia hit again by a shareholder lawsuit over its CEO's alleged links to a suspected Chinese agent. In Asia, strong AI-chip demand, shown by TSMC's 60% jump in monthly sales, lifted Taiwan, Korea and Japan. Oil bounced off a two-month low because ships are still being hit in the Strait of Hormuz even as Washington talks of the Iran war being over. Beyond markets, Congo's Ebola outbreak passed 11,000 cases, the second-largest ever recorded, and Russia, Ukraine and the US hold a second day of talks in Abu Dhabi focused on a large prisoner exchange, while Poland marks Independence Day.

glossary.def: The interest rate the US government pays when it borrows by selling bonds; it rises when bond prices fall.
glossary.example: The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.99% on 10 November.

glossary.def: A government's budget balance excluding interest payments on its debt; it shows what current policy is doing.
glossary.example: The US primary deficit in fiscal 2026 was about $0.85 trillion.

glossary.def: Government debt divided by a year's GDP, used to compare debt burdens across countries.
glossary.example: Poland's general government debt was 59.6% of GDP in 2025 (Eurostat).

glossary.def: The EU process that pushes a country whose deficit or debt breaks the 3% or 60% reference values to correct it, with possible sanctions.
glossary.example: Poland has been under an EDP since 26 July 2024.

glossary.def: The extra price or return demanded to compensate for a possible bad outcome, such as a supply disruption.
glossary.example: Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz keep a risk premium in oil prices.

glossary.def: Using warships to stop ships from entering or leaving a country's ports.
glossary.example: The US keeps a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

glossary.def: A contract clause that excuses a party from its obligations when events beyond its control, such as war, prevent it from performing.
glossary.example: QatarEnergy has been under force majeure on LNG deliveries since spring 2026.

glossary.def: Natural gas cooled to about −162°C so it becomes liquid and can be shipped by tanker.
glossary.example: Orlen cancelled a contract for 1 million tonnes of Qatari LNG a year.

glossary.def: A company that manufactures chips designed by other firms.
glossary.example: TSMC is the world's leading chip foundry.

glossary.def: A lawsuit filed by one or a few people on behalf of a larger group with the same claim.
glossary.example: An Nvidia shareholder seeks class-action status for investors who bought between 9 October and 8 November.

glossary.def: The formal process in which a legislature charges an official with wrongdoing; in the US the House impeaches and the Senate holds the trial.
glossary.example: The House shelved articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Hegseth.

glossary.def: Replacing fuels burned directly (petrol, gas, coal) with electricity, for example electric cars and heat pumps.
glossary.example: Türkiye proposes raising electricity to 35% of global energy use by 2035.

glossary.def: The total amount of CO2 that can still be emitted while keeping warming below a given limit such as 1.5°C.
glossary.example: Scientists estimate 150 billion tonnes remain for 1.5°C, less than four years of current emissions.

glossary.def: A bacterial disease spread by contaminated water or food that causes severe diarrhoea; it is treatable with oral rehydration and antibiotics.
glossary.example: Congo has recorded more than 60,000 cholera cases this year.

glossary.def: Research that watches what happens to people without assigning treatments, so it can show links but not prove cause and effect.
glossary.example: The Italian GLP-1 study linked stopping the drugs to higher heart risk but could not prove causation.

stories.title: Fed officials open the door to a half-point rate rise in December; the US 10-year bond yield jumps to nearly 5%
stories.what: After Tuesday's hotter-than-expected US inflation report, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point hike (0.5 percentage point) should be considered at the 8–9 December meeting, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said it may be possible to move faster than September's quarter-point rise, Reuters reported. Traders saw a quarter-point hike as all but certain and, by Tuesday midmorning in New York, put the chance of a half-point move at close to 15%. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury bond rose to 4.99% from 4.88% on Monday (AP), and the 2-year yield, which tracks expectations for Fed rates, had its biggest one-day rise since early April 2025 (Reuters). The Fed's key rate is currently 3.75%–4.00%.
stories.why: 'Core' prices (excluding food and energy) rose 0.3% in October for a third straight month, above the 0.2% forecast; Waller had said a 0.3% reading would make him back a bigger move, and Logan called the current rate range too low, saying it adds to inflationary pressures (Reuters). When investors expect higher policy rates, they demand higher yields on government bonds, so bond prices fall. According to the dpa-AFX news agency, European shares took the news calmly because a December hike was already largely priced in.

stories.everyday: Brent drives what refiners pay for crude, so these swings reach Polish petrol stations and heating-oil bills with a lag of days to weeks. The mines and attacks mean a risk premium in prices can last even if diplomacy progresses.
stories.rankWhy: About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so continuing attacks on tankers keep energy prices high and volatile for every importing country.

stories.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say two tankers caught fire on a 'forbidden' Hormuz route; oil bounces off a two-month low
stories.what: On Tuesday the navy of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two oil tankers that had switched off their tracking systems caught fire on what Iran calls an unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz: one, it said, hit naval mines; the other was set ablaze after an unspecified 'incident' while, it claimed, US fighter jets were protecting it (Xinhua, Middle East Eye). These are Iranian claims; no ship names, flags or casualties were given and they have not been independently confirmed. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported another tanker struck north-east of Lima in Oman on Tuesday, and the Washington Institute for Near East Policy counted 37 attacks on ships in and near the strait in October, the most of any month since the war began, and 10 so far in November (Reuters). Brent crude rose 0.8% to $92.20 a barrel by 02:19 Warsaw time on Wednesday after hitting a two-month low on Tuesday.
stories.why: Iran has restricted passage through the strait since 28 February, when US and Israeli strikes started the war, and the US keeps a naval blockade of Iranian ports. Prices swing between peace hopes, after President Trump said on Monday the war was 'militarily' effectively over, and the reality of attacks on shipping. Analysts at LSEG wrote that even with a deal, more oil would flow only after mines are cleared and insurance costs and shipowners' fears ease (Reuters).

stories.everyday: Ebola spreads through direct contact with the body fluids of sick people, not through the air, so the risk to people in Europe remains very low. The human cost is concentrated in eastern Congo, where families also face war and displacement.
stories.rankWhy: The second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded has killed more than 5,300 people and has spread to East, Central and West Africa, with no specific vaccine or treatment.

stories.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 11,000 cases and 5,387 deaths, the second-largest on record
stories.what: Congo has recorded 11,042 Ebola cases and at least 5,387 deaths since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, according to health-ministry figures reported on 11 November (AP, Al Jazeera). It is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which no vaccine or treatment has been specifically developed, and which kills about half of those it infects. Eight of Congo's 26 provinces are affected, with Ituri and North Kivu the hotspots, and cases have also been reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. Only the 2014–2016 West African outbreak (more than 28,600 cases and more than 11,000 deaths) was larger. Earlier in November the WHO approved clinical trials of two new Ebola vaccines, with results expected in early 2027.
stories.why: AP and Al Jazeera report that armed conflict, including renewed violence in Ituri and North Kivu, attacks on health workers and facilities, poor roads, a strained health system and mistrust have delayed detection and let the virus spread faster than in past outbreaks. Many deaths are happening outside treatment centres, which makes tracing contacts harder. Health authorities are calling for a halt to fighting so that health workers can reach the sick.

stories.everyday: A prisoner exchange would bring thousands of soldiers and civilians home to their families. For Poland, which hosts many Ukrainian refugees and borders both countries, a durable settlement would change security, defence spending and reconstruction business.
stories.rankWhy: Any progress toward ending Europe's largest war since 1945 would affect the security, energy prices and budgets of the whole continent, Poland above all.

stories.title: Russia–Ukraine–US talks in Abu Dhabi enter a second day, with a large prisoner exchange of 1,000 or 1,500 per side on the table
stories.what: The first US-mediated three-way talks since February ran for about four hours on Tuesday (AP); Russia's TASS put it at four and a half hours including a break. Russia's team was led by Vladimir Medinsky, Ukraine's by Rustem Umerov, and the US was represented by Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the sides discussed a 'large-scale' prisoner exchange of 1,000 for 1,000, possibly 1,500 for 1,500, which the Americans would take to Moscow, and that Wednesday's main day would cover de-escalation, energy, the Black Sea, the exchange and a possible three-way leaders' meeting. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the talks 'very productive' but said a solution was not imminent.
stories.why: The positions on the core issue remain far apart: Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to withdraw from four regions Russia claims to have annexed but has not fully captured, to drop its NATO bid and accept military limits, while Kyiv rejects giving up territory and wants an immediate ceasefire (AP). Zelensky said Russia raised territory and that this belongs at leaders' level. AP notes that pressure on Russia's wartime economy, the US midterm results and Russia's winter strikes on Ukraine's power grid have changed the backdrop.

stories.rankWhy: TSMC makes most of the world's advanced chips, so its sales are a real-time gauge of the AI boom that drives stock markets from Taipei and Seoul to New York.

stories.title: TSMC's October sales jump 60% and it will invest up to $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI; Asian chip stocks surge
stories.what: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) reported October revenue of NT$586.89 billion, up 59.7% from a year earlier and 14.7% from September, its filing to the US Securities and Exchange Commission shows. Its board also approved buying up to $500 million of Anthropic shares at the IPO price and up to $500 million of OpenAI preferred stock, plus about $40.9 billion of capital spending. On Wednesday Taiwan's Taiex rose 3.6%, South Korea's Kospi 2.4% to 5,365.75 and Japan's Nikkei 225 1.3% to 61,248.59; Samsung Electronics gained 3.4%, SK hynix 5.4% and TSMC 3.1% (AP). Hong Kong's Hang Seng was the exception, down 0.7%.
stories.why: AP attributed the gains to solid demand for AI chips, which outweighed Wall Street's fall on inflation worries. Rising monthly sales at the main chip foundry suggest that companies are still spending heavily on AI data centres despite recent doubts about AI valuations. Chip makers investing in their own customers, such as AI developers, also ties their fortunes more closely together.

stories.everyday: Global index funds and many Polish pension and investment funds hold large positions in US tech, so a fall in Nvidia shows up in their values. The case also shows how personal conduct of a CEO can become a company risk.
stories.rankWhy: Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable companies and the heaviest weight in US indices, so its slide drags on the savings of millions of index investors.

stories.title: Wall Street closes lower after the inflation surprise; Nvidia falls again as a shareholder sues over its CEO's alleged links to a suspected Chinese agent
stories.what: The S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,520.93 on Tuesday, the Dow Jones 0.3% to 52,231.89 and the Nasdaq Composite 0.7% to 25,065.87, though all remain higher for the week and the year (AP). Nvidia was the biggest drag on the S&P 500, falling 5.5% according to AP. A retail investor, Mark Kistenmacher, filed a lawsuit in California on Monday seeking class-action status, alleging Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang misled investors by not disclosing Huang's relationship with a woman news reports say is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, and about a Singapore company linked to her (AP via PBS). Nvidia's board is investigating, President Trump said the FBI is looking into the matter, and Huang has acknowledged the affair, apologised and said he will cooperate.
stories.why: Shares fell because the inflation report raised bets on Fed rate hikes, and higher rates make future company profits worth less today, hitting expensive tech stocks hardest (AP). For Nvidia, investors also weigh legal and reputational risk and the national-security questions raised by the allegations, which the lawsuit calls material risks to the business.

stories.everyday: Decisions on electrification and fossil fuels feed into EU rules that shape Poland's coal phase-out, heating costs and car prices over the coming years.
stories.rankWhy: The yearly UN climate summit shapes how fast nearly 200 countries cut emissions, but the absence of most big-economy leaders limits what this round can deliver.

stories.title: COP31 leaders' summit opens in Antalya, but most big-economy leaders stay away; Türkiye pushes a global electrification goal
stories.what: World leaders address the COP31 UN climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, on Wednesday and Thursday; the talks run from 9 to 20 November. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is the only G7 leader scheduled to speak; France's Emmanuel Macron, Germany's Friedrich Merz and Italy's Giorgia Meloni are skipping it, US President Donald Trump is not attending, and China is represented by Vice President Han Zheng (AFP via RTÉ). Brazil's Lula da Silva, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen are among those attending. The host is seeking support for a voluntary goal to raise electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035.
stories.why: Electrification means replacing fuels burned directly in transport, buildings and industry with electricity, for example electric cars and heat pumps. The EU insists the electricity must be 'clean', which could reopen arguments over oil, gas and coal; countries agreed in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels but have struggled to advance that goal since (AFP). EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra said expectations are 'not necessarily high'.

stories.everyday: A one-year dip does not stop warming: CO2 keeps accumulating as long as emissions are above zero. That is why heatwaves, floods and fires keep becoming more frequent, including in Central Europe.
stories.rankWhy: The most-watched annual scientific estimate of global CO2 emissions shows the first fall in fossil emissions in years, but total CO2 still rising, framing every climate negotiation.

stories.title: Scientists project that fossil-fuel CO2 emissions will fall 0.4% in 2026, helped by solar, wind and the Iran war, while total CO2 still rises
stories.what: The Global Carbon Project's annual report, published on 10 November, projects fossil CO2 emissions of 38.2 billion tonnes in 2026, down 0.4%. China's emissions are projected to fall 0.9%, the US's 1.3% and the EU's 1.5%, while India's rise 4.4%. Emissions from oil are expected to drop 1.9%. But total CO2 emissions, including land use, are projected to rise to 43.3 billion tonnes from 42.8 billion, because of peat fires and forest damage in Southeast Asia.
